title: Chapter 1 – Introduction to the Human Body
notes: Anatomy studies structure; Physiology studies function.
Levels of organization: chemical → cellular → tissue → organ → system → organism.
Eleven systems: integumentary, skeletal, muscular, nervous, endocrine, cardiovascular, lymphatic/immune, respiratory, digestive, urinary, reproductive.
Life processes: metabolism, responsiveness, movement, growth, differentiation, reproduction.
Homeostasis is dynamic balance maintained by nervous and endocrine control.
Negative feedback reduces deviations from a set point (e.g., thermoregulation).
Positive feedback amplifies a change (e.g., oxytocin during labor).
Components of a feedback loop: receptor, control center, effector.
Anatomical position: standing upright, face forward, arms at sides, palms forward, feet flat.
Directional terms: superior/inferior; anterior/posterior; medial/lateral; proximal/distal; superficial/deep.
Body planes: sagittal (mid/para), frontal (coronal), transverse (horizontal), oblique.
Dorsal cavity: cranial + vertebral canal; Ventral cavity: thoracic + abdominopelvic.
Serous membranes: parietal vs visceral layers; pleura, pericardium, peritoneum.
Abdominopelvic regions (9) and quadrants (4) standardize localization.
Diaphragm separates thoracic and abdominopelvic cavities.
Retroperitoneal organs lie posterior to the peritoneum (e.g., kidneys).
Serous fluid reduces friction between moving organs.
Imaging: X‑ray, CT, MRI, PET, ultrasound—distinct advantages and limitations.
Aging reduces homeostatic efficiency and repair capacity.
Extracellular fluid (ECF) surrounds cells and must be tightly regulated.
Regional names (cephalic, brachial, femoral, etc.) enable precise references.
Mediastinum contains heart, trachea, esophagus, major vessels; pericardial cavity within.
Clinical: failure of homeostasis leads to disorder, disease, or death.
Prone vs supine describe body position when reclining.
CT provides cross‑sectional X‑ray; MRI uses magnetic fields; PET maps metabolic activity.
Surface anatomy references landmarks for clinical procedures.
Terminology consistency is critical for communication in healthcare.
